body_text: View All News NETSCOUT Extends Adaptive DDoS Defense Protection to Address the Rising Business Cost of Weaponized Broadband and IoT Devices August 18, 2026 Download (opens in new window) New Automated Outbound Protection Helps Service Providers Reduce Network Disruption, Infrastructure Costs and Internet-Wide Risk WESTFORD, Mass.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- NETSCOUT® (NASDAQ: NTCT), a leading provider of observability, AIOps, cybersecurity, and DDoS attack protection solutions, today announced an extension of its Adaptive DDoS Protection (ADP) solution enabling service providers to automatically detect and mitigate outbound DDoS attack traffic. By extending protection from the attack target towards its source, NETSCOUT helps operators prevent compromised subscriber devices from disrupting their own networks, consuming costly capacity and attacking customers and organizations across the internet. Consumer broadband routers, cameras and other IoT devices are increasingly being weaponized by Turbo-Mirai class botnets capable of generating multi-terabit attacks. These outbound attacks have already caused costly service outages, reputational damage and customer loss, and damage to peering relationships risking a large increase in transit costs at service providers around the world. By detecting and mitigating malicious traffic generated by compromised device populations before it leaves their networks, service providers can reduce abuse complaints and infrastructure costs while protecting their own networks and services and helping lower subscriber churn and regulatory risk. “The combination of higher-speed broadband connectivity and vulnerable IoT devices has been weaponized by a new class of massive DDoS botnets,” said Patrick Donegan, founder and principal analyst, HardenStance. “Source-side mitigation, or attack suppression as it’s sometimes known, is a critical part of the equation. NETSCOUT’s approach, backed by its ATLAS Intelligence Feed (AIF) and ASERT analysts, gives service providers the tools they need to detect and stop attacks before they have an impact, protecting their customers and the broader internet from the large-scale DDoS attacks we have seen.” Using AI-powered threat intelligence and automated detection and mitigation, NETSCOUT’s ADP solution, an addition to its Arbor Sightline and Arbor Threat Mitigation System : Automatically detects and mitigates ever evolving attacks through dynamic detection, intelligent redirection and adaptive mitigation. Extends these capabilities to outbound traffic, combining enhanced, customized detection with comprehensive threat intelligence tailored for each ISP. Uses NETSCOUT’s proprietary AI/ML-powered DDoS detection to analyze massive volumes of outbound internet traffic to uncover attacks designed to hide within legitimate flows. Draws on unique global real-time intelligence of DDoS activity covering approximately half of all internet traffic to rapidly detect and mitigate DDoS attacks and pinpoint the responsible, compromised devices. “We are extending DDoS defense from the target to the source,” stated Darren Anstee, CTO, Security, NETSCOUT. “By using our internet-scale visibility to derive localized threat intelligence for our customers, NETSCOUT can identify and precisely suppress attacks at their origin, before they cause problems locally or at their target. This capability gives our customers a new level of comprehensive defense across their peering, transit, cloud and customer edges.” This expansion of capabilities demonstrates how NETSCOUT is applying its global threat visibility and proven ADP solution to meet emerging service provider challenges. By extending an established inbound DDoS workflow to outbound and cross-bound threats, NETSCOUT enables operators to improve network-resilience, cost-controls and revenue protection through its proven Arbor Sightline and Arbor TMS solutions. Resources: Learn more about the expanded Arbor Sightline and the Arbor Threat Mitigation System . Understand the evolving tactics of botnet-driven DDoS from the latest NETSCOUT DDoS Threat Intelligence Report . About NETSCOUT NETSCOUT SYSTEMS, INC. (NASDAQ: NTCT) protects the connected world from cyberattacks and performance and availability disruptions through its unique visibility platform and solutions powered by its pioneering deep packet inspection at scale technology. As a leading provider of network observability, AIOps, carrier service assurance, cybersecurity, and Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack protection solutions, NETSCOUT serves the world’s largest enterprises, service providers, and public sector organizations. title: The Psychology of Overconfidence: Why Self-Belief Can Lead to Success

body_text: Discover why people tend to be overconfident, how self-belief may have evolved, and what psychology research reveals about confidence, risk-taking and success. Why Are People So Confident in Their Abilities? Confidence is usually considered a positive quality. It can encourage people to pursue ambitious goals, start businesses, take on leadership roles and compete when others might hesitate. But confidence can also go too far. Many people believe they are better than average at driving, intelligence, communication or other everyday skills. Statistically, everyone cannot be above average. This widespread tendency raises an interesting question: if overconfidence can lead to poor decisions, financial losses and unnecessary risks, why has it remained such a common feature of human behaviour? New research offers an intriguing explanation. Rather than viewing excessive confidence purely as a psychological mistake, researchers suggest that self-belief may also function as a social signal. In other words, confidence may sometimes communicate something about a person's underlying ability. Overconfidence May Have an Evolutionary Advantage One influential explanation for human self-deception comes from evolutionary biology. The basic idea is that people who genuinely believe in their own abilities may appear more convincing to others. Someone who is nervous, hesitant or visibly uncertain can unintentionally reveal that they do not fully believe what they are saying. By contrast, genuine self-belief can make communication appear more persuasive. However, researchers Chris Dawson and David de Meza argue that this explanation does not tell the whole story. If everyone simply becomes more confident, why would confidence remain a useful signal? Their theory draws on the biological concept known as the handicap principle . A famous example is the peacock's elaborate tail. The tail requires resources to develop and can make the bird less agile. Because maintaining such a costly feature is easier for a healthy, capable bird, the display can provide information about the animal's condition. The researchers suggest that extreme self-belief can operate in a somewhat similar way. Confidence Can Be Costly Imagine two drivers. One is an inexperienced beginner who believes they are an exceptional driver. The consequences of that confidence could be serious because their actual ability is not strong enough to support their belief. The second driver is highly skilled but equally confident. Their strong self-belief is less likely to produce disastrous consequences because they possess the ability to back it up. This creates an interesting relationship between confidence and competence. For capable people, confidence can provide significant advantages while carrying relatively manageable costs. Confidence may encourage them to apply for opportunities, negotiate, compete, launch projects or take calculated risks. For less capable people, the same level of confidence may produce much greater consequences. This difference can make confidence a potentially informative signal of ability, even when confidence itself is not perfectly accurate. The Dunning-Kruger Effect May Be More Complicated Than We Think The discussion of overconfidence often leads to the Dunning-Kruger effect , a concept introduced by psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger. Their influential research suggested that people with lower levels of competence can sometimes be particularly poor at recognising their own mistakes. In simple terms, someone may lack both the skills needed to perform well and the knowledge required to recognise their weaknesses. This idea became widely popular as the phrase "unskilled and unaware of it." However, interpreting these findings is more complicated than the popular version suggests. One important statistical issue involves randomness. When people are divided according to their actual test results, individuals who perform poorly may have been affected by bad luck as well as ability. Their predictions about their performance cannot perfectly account for random factors. Researchers can approach the problem differently by grouping participants according to their expectations rather than their eventual test scores. According to the research discussed by Dawson and de Meza, people with higher expectations also tended to perform better while displaying greater overconfidence overall. This interpretation challenges the simplistic idea that the most confident people are necessarily the least competent. Why Confidence Can Help People Take Opportunities Self-belief can have practical benefits. A person who believes they can succeed may be more willing to enter a competitive environment. They might apply for a demanding job, pitch an idea, start a company or pursue a difficult personal goal. Someone who accurately recognises every possible obstacle may sometimes become so cautious that they never take action. This creates an important distinction between confidence and accuracy . Confidence does not guarantee success. However, a certain level of confidence can influence whether a person gets the opportunity to demonstrate their abilities in the first place. That may help explain why excessive confidence can persist even when it occasionally produces spectacular mistakes. The Role of Loss Aversion Another psychological trait complicates the picture: loss aversion . People often react more strongly to losses than to equivalent gains. Losing a certain amount of money can feel more painful than gaining the same amount feels rewarding. This can encourage cautious behaviour. At first, loss aversion appears to contradict the idea that humans benefit from overconfidence. If people are extremely worried about losing, why would they confidently take risks? The answer may be that human psychology does not perfectly balance confidence and caution in every situation. People face countless decisions involving careers, investments, relationships, competition and business. It would be extremely difficult to calculate exactly how much confidence and caution should be applied to every individual situation. As a result, the two tendencies can coexist. A person may be highly confident about their abilities while simultaneously being reluctant to accept certain risks. When Overconfidence Becomes Dangerous Although confidence can provide advantages, excessive self-belief can also become destructive. Overconfidence can contribute to: Poor investment decisions Risky driving Failed business ventures Unrealistic plans Bad leadership decisions Underestimating competitors Ignoring useful criticism Taking unnecessary personal risks The problem is not confidence itself. The danger appears when confidence becomes disconnected from evidence. Healthy confidence says, "I believe I can handle this." Unhealthy overconfidence says, "There is no realistic possibility that I could be wrong." That distinction matters. How to Build Better Confidence The goal should not necessarily be to eliminate confidence. Instead, people can try to make their confidence better calibrated. One useful approach is to deliberately consider evidence that challenges your assumptions. Before making an important decision, ask: What could I be missing? What evidence would prove me wrong? Have I underestimated the risks? What would someone with more experience say? These questions do not require abandoning self-belief. They simply create space for reality to challenge your expectations. Confidence works best when it is combined with feedback, experience and a willingness to reconsider mistakes. The Bigger Lesson About Human Behaviour The psychology of overconfidence reveals something important about how people operate. Human behaviour is not always designed to produce perfectly accurate beliefs. Sometimes beliefs may serve social, motivational or evolutionary functions as well. Confidence can encourage action. It can influence how others perceive us. It can help us pursue opportunities that we might otherwise avoid. But the same mechanism can become dangerous when confidence grows faster than competence. Perhaps the healthiest approach is therefore neither extreme humility nor blind self-belief. Instead, aim for informed confidence : believe in your ability to improve and succeed, while remaining willing to question your assumptions. After all, confidence can open a door, but ability, preparation and good judgement determine what happens after you walk through it. Source The Conversation UK on August 7, 2026, by Chris Dawson, Professor of Economics and Behavioural Science at the University of Bath, and David de Meza, Professor of Management at the London School of Economics and Political Science. It is a written summary and interpretation of published research and should not be treated as professional psychological, financial, medical or investment advice. Research findings can be more nuanced than a general-audience summary, and individual behaviour can vary considerably. Readers should consult appropriate qualified professionals when making important personal, financial or professional decisions.

title: Golar LNG announces a new $600 million senior secured Revolving Credit Facility
summary: Golar LNG Limited (“Golar”) is pleased to announce successful closing of a new $600 million senior secured Revolving Credit Facility (“RCF”). The RCF...
body_text: Golar LNG Limited (“Golar”) is pleased to announce successful closing of a new $600 million senior secured Revolving Credit Facility (“RCF”). The RCF further strengthens Golar’s balance sheet flexibility and facilitates for further FLNG growth. The RCF is secured by Golar’s investment in the MKII FLNG currently being converted in China to serve a 20-year contract with Southern Energy S.A. in Argentina. The facility received strong backing from a consortium of banks including ABN AMRO, Citibank, Danske Bank and Standard Chartered Bank. title: Aramark Collegiate Hospitality Selected to Transform Campus Dining and Hospitality Services at University of Colorado Colorado Springs
summary: The Investor Relations website contains information about Aramark's business for stockholders, potential investors, and financial analysts.
body_text: PDF Version New partnership brings innovative campus dining, retail, catering, and hospitality solutions to enhance the student experience at UCCS PHILADELPHIA--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 5, 2026-- Aramark Collegiate Hospitality, a leading provider of higher education dining and hospitality services, today announced a new long-term partnership with the University of Colorado Colorado Springs (UCCS) to operate and enhance campus dining, retail dining, catering, and hospitality programs across the university. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260805758975/en/ The partnership represents Aramark Collegiate Hospitality's first collaboration within the University of Colorado System , strengthening the company's growing presence in Colorado and expanding its commitment to supporting public higher education institutions through innovative campus dining solutions and student-centered hospitality programs. "UCCS's commitment to innovation and student success makes them an ideal partner for Aramark," said Barbara Flanagan, President and CEO of Aramark Collegiate Hospitality . "Together, we're creating a dining and hospitality program that reflects the unique culture of the Mountain Lion community while preparing for the future of higher education dining. As Gen Alpha students begin arriving on college campuses in the years ahead, expectations around wellness, convenience, personalization, and meaningful dining experiences will continue to evolve. Our partnership positions UCCS at the forefront of those changes." UCCS selected Aramark Collegiate Hospitality based on a shared commitment to student success, operational excellence, and collaborative innovation. The new dining program will introduce enhanced retail dining options, expanded food and beverage offerings, strategic partnerships with national and local restaurant brands, and opportunities for student-developed concepts and entrepreneurial initiatives. In addition to elevating campus dining, the partnership will expand community-building experiences through themed events, cultural celebrations, social dining programs, and hospitality experiences designed to increase student engagement and campus connection. "At UCCS, we are committed to providing a university experience that supports our students in every aspect of campus life," said University of Colorado Colorado Springs Chancellor Jennifer Sobanet . "Dining is an important part of that experience, and our partnership with Aramark reflects that commitment by bringing more variety, new concepts, and continued enhancements to dining on campus. We look forward to working together to further enrich the UCCS experience." Through the partnership, Aramark Collegiate Hospitality and UCCS will create customized hospitality experiences that serve the needs of a growing and diverse community of students, faculty, staff, and campus visitors. The program will combine Aramark's proprietary dining concepts with national brands, local restaurants, and regional food partners to deliver a campus dining experience that reflects the character of Colorado Springs and the UCCS community. Menus and dining solutions will prioritize food quality, convenience, health and wellness, sustainability, and menu variety. Technology-enabled tools and digital solutions will support a seamless guest experience while improving operational efficiency and service delivery throughout campus dining locations. Aramark Collegiate Hospitality will also oversee catering and event hospitality services across campus, including operations at the Ent Center for the Performing Arts , further enhancing the university's ability to serve students, faculty, guests, and community partners. About University of Colorado Colorado Springs The University of Colorado Colorado Springs (UCCS) is a public research university located in Colorado Springs and part of the University of Colorado System. Home to more than 11,300 students and more than 800 faculty members, UCCS offers more than 140 degree programs across six colleges and schools. With a focus on innovation, access, research, and student success, UCCS provides a vibrant campus experience in the heart of Colorado Springs and prepares students for meaningful careers, continued education, and lifelong impact. About Aramark Collegiate Hospitality Aramark Collegiate Hospitality —where futures are better served—has been a trusted dining partner to higher education institutions for over 50 years. Serving approximately 300 colleges and universities nationwide, Aramark delivers customized dining and hospitality programs that reflect the unique culture and needs of each campus. Rooted in a deep commitment to service for people, partners, the community, and the planet, Aramark goes beyond meals by curating tailored experiences, supporting success, and cultivating communities. title: Everspin Reports Unaudited Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results
summary: CHANDLER, Ariz. --(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 5, 2026-- Everspin Technologies, Inc. (NASDAQ: MRAM), the world’s leading developer and manufacturer of Magnetoresistive Random Access Memory (MRAM) persistent memory solutions, today announced preliminary unaudited financial results for the second quarter
body_text: CHANDLER, Ariz.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 5, 2026-- Everspin Technologies, Inc. (NASDAQ: MRAM), the world’s leading developer and manufacturer of Magnetoresistive Random Access Memory (MRAM) persistent memory solutions, today announced preliminary unaudited financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. “Our second quarter results were driven by strong product revenue coupled with initial non-product revenue under our recently signed $40 million contract with a US prime contractor. From an end market perspective, growth was led by strength in Industrial Automation, Energy Management, and Aerospace and Defense,” said Sanjeev Aggarwal, President and Chief Executive Officer. “We continue to see strong growth across our existing business while executing on our product pipeline and developing solutions that will further expand Everspin's addressable market and drive long-term growth.” Second Quarter 2026 Results Total revenue of $18.7 million, compared to $13.2 million in the second quarter of 2025. MRAM product sales, which include both Toggle and STT-MRAM revenue, of $15.3 million, compared to $11.1 million in the second quarter of 2025. Licensing, royalty, engineering services and other revenue of $3.4 million, compared to $2.1 million in the second quarter of 2025. Gross margin of 53.9%, compared to 51.3% in the second quarter of 2025. GAAP operating expenses of $14.5 million, compared to $8.7 million in the second quarter of 2025. Interest and Other income, net of $0.8 million, compared to $1.3 million in the second quarter of 2025. GAAP net loss of $(3.6) million, or $(0.15) per diluted share, compared to net loss of $(0.7) million, or $(0.03) per diluted share, in the second quarter of 2025. Non-GAAP net income of $2.9 million, or $0.11 per diluted share, compared to non-GAAP net income of $0.7 million, or $0.03 per diluted share, in the second quarter of 2025. Cash and cash equivalents as of June 30, 2026, totaled $43.9 million. “We are pleased to report record quarterly revenue with second quarter results above our expectations, driven by both strong product and non-product revenue growth. We remain focused on balancing strategic investments in our technology roadmap with prudent expense management, strengthening our competitive position while enhancing long-term shareholder value,” said Bill Cooper, Everspin’s Chief Financial Officer. Business Outlook For the third quarter of 2026, Everspin expects total revenue in a range of $19.5 million to $20.5 million and GAAP net loss per share to be between ($0.10) and ($0.05). Non-GAAP net income per diluted share is anticipated to be between $0.10 and $0.15. A reconciliation of non-GAAP guidance measures to corresponding GAAP guidance measures is not available on a forward-looking basis without unreasonable effort due to the uncertainty regarding, and the potential variability of, expenses that may be incurred in the future. For example, stock-based compensation-related charges are impacted by the timing of employee stock transactions, the future fair market value of Everspin’s common stock, and Everspin’s future hiring and retention needs, all of which are difficult to predict and subject to constant change. Additionally, litigation expenses are highly dependent on case related activity in any given period and based on the actions of a third-party which are difficult to predict and subject to change. These factors could be material to Everspin’s results computed in accordance with GAAP. This outlook is dependent on Everspin's current expectations, which may be impacted by, among other things, evolving external conditions, such as public health-related events or outbreaks, local safety guidelines, worsening impacts due to supply chain constraints or interruptions, including general market and semiconductor industry volatility, and the other risk factors described in Everspin's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the "SEC"), including its Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025, its Quarterly Reports on Form 10-Q filed with the SEC during 2026, as well as in its subsequent filings with the SEC. Use of Non-GAAP Financial Measures Everspin supplements the reporting of its financial information determined under generally accepted accounting principles in the United States of America (GAAP) with Non-GAAP financial measures including gross profit, gross margin, operating expenses, operating income (loss), operating margin, net income (loss), and EPS which are defined as the GAAP financial measures excluding the effect of stock-based compensation, non-recurring engineering expenses related to the company's foundry agreement with Microchip and litigation costs. Everspin’s GAAP tax rate is effectively zero due to NOL carryforwards, thus a Non-GAAP tax rate is not included as a Non-GAAP financial measure. Everspin’s management and board of directors use these non-GAAP measures to understand and evaluate its operating performance and trends, to prepare and approve its annual budget and to develop short-term and long-term operating and financing plans. Accordingly, Everspin believes that these non-GAAP measures provide useful information for investors in understanding and evaluating its operating results in the same manner as its management and board of directors. These non-GAAP financial measures should be considered in addition to, not as superior to, or as a substitute for, financial measures reported in accordance with GAAP. Moreover, other companies may define these non-GAAP measures differently, which limits the usefulness of this measure for comparisons with such other companies. Everspin encourages investors to review its financial statements and publicly filed reports in their entirety and not to rely on any single financial measure. Please see the tables included at the end of this release for the reconciliation of GAAP to non-GAAP results. Conference Call Everspin will host a conference call for analysts and investors on Wednesday, August 5th, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time. Dial-in details: To access the call by phone, please go to this link and you will be provided with dial-in details. To avoid delays, we encourage participants to dial into the conference call fifteen minutes ahead of the scheduled start time. The live webcast of the call will be accessible on Everspin’s website at investor.everspin.com . Approximately two hours after the conclusion of the live event, an archived webcast of the conference call will be accessible from the Investor Relations section of Everspin’s website for twelve months. Everspin MRAM delivers the industry’s most robust, highest-performance non-volatile memory for industrial, data center, automotive, aerospace and other mission-critical applications where data persistence is essential. title: GovDash vs GovEagle: Full Lifecycle Comparison (Aug 2026)
summary: GovDash vs GovEagle August 2026: A direct look at features, security, and lifecycle coverage to help government contractors choose the right tool.
body_text: If your team is still juggling separate systems for capture, proposals, and contract tracking, you know how much gets lost in the handoffs between them. The choice between GovEagle and GovDash comes down to whether you want to fill one of those gaps or close all of them at once. This comparison lays out exactly what each product covers so you can make that call with a clear picture. TL;DR: GovEagle focuses on RFP shredding, compliance matrix generation, and proposal narrative drafting, with no capture management, pricing, or contract management modules. GovDash connects BD, capture, proposal development, Pricer, and contract management in one system, so data carries across the full pursuit lifecycle without re-entry. Compliance matrix build drops from 8 to 14 hours down to under 2 hours per solicitation with GovDash's automated Section L and M extraction. GovEagle references NIST 800-53 alignment and is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate Equivalency, but has not completed a C3PAO audit or earned formal FedRAMP authorization, which matters for teams with ATO-dependent requirements. GovDash is the AI platform for winning government contracts, covering every stage from pipeline to post-award in one place. What is GovEagle? GovEagle is an AI-powered tool built for government contractors, covering RFP shredding, compliance matrix generation, and proposal narrative drafting. It helps teams build compliance matrices, generate annotated outlines, and surface relevant past performance and incumbent data to support bid decisions. The tool works natively inside Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and SharePoint, which keeps it accessible for teams already running proposals through that stack. Where GovEagle draws a clear boundary is scope. It is purpose-built for proposal work and does not extend into capture management, contract administration, pricing, or BD pipeline tracking. For contractors who want a focused writing aid that plugs into their existing Microsoft environment without requiring a broader workflow change, that narrow focus can be a reasonable fit. The practical trade-off is that teams using GovEagle still need separate systems to manage opportunities upstream and contracts downstream, which means data does not carry across the full pursuit lifecycle in one place. What is GovDash? GovDash is the AI platform for winning government contracts, connecting opportunity discovery, capture, pricing, proposal development, and post-award contract management in one system. Dash, the AI agent, and the Data Library run across every module, so the intelligence your team builds during capture carries forward into proposals and beyond. Here is what that looks like in practice across the core workflow areas: Opportunity discovery pulls relevant solicitations automatically, so BD teams spend less time scanning SAM.gov and more time assessing fit against their win criteria. Capture management ties pursuit data directly to proposal inputs, so nothing gets lost between the pipeline and the writing phase. Proposal development generates compliant first drafts grounded in your Data Library, cutting first-draft time from several days down to hours without sacrificing technical accuracy. Pricer handles cost volume construction with the rigor federal price to win strategies require. Contract management tracks deliverables, modifications, and obligations post-award, eliminating hours of manual cross-referencing each week. With 54% of the GovDash team coming from GovCon roles, the product is built around how federal contractors actually work, not around generic enterprise workflows adapted after the fact. Proposal Development and Compliance Workflow GovDash reads the PWS, extracts every requirement, and maps each one against your compliance matrix automatically. From there, the system generates section-by-section outlines tied directly to Sections L and M, so writers know exactly what evaluators are scoring before a single word goes down. The proposal development workflow pulls from your Data Library, meaning past performance entries, technical approaches, and management narratives are surfaced in context instead of buried in a shared drive. First-draft generation for technical volumes drops from three to five days down to four to eight hours, freeing senior SMEs to focus on review and refinement instead of writing from scratch. For a deeper look at how this works, see our AI proposal development guide . Compliance matrix automation runs continuously. GovDash flags missing requirements, page limit violations, and Section M criteria gaps as writers work, instead of surfacing those issues at the Pink or Red Team stage. Proposal Workflow Capability GovDash GovEagle Compliance matrix build time Under 2 hours (automated) Yes (automated) Section L and M extraction Automated Partial Continuous amendment tracking Yes Not documented First-draft generation (technical volumes) 4-8 hours Yes (narrative generation) Data Library grounding Yes (firm past performance, resumes, technical content) Limited Annotated outline generation Yes Yes Live compliance gap flagging during writing Yes No Where GovEagle Focuses GovEagle's proposal-related features focus on RFP shredding, compliance matrix generation, and narrative drafting. The product surfaces relevant past performance and incumbent data to inform bid decisions, and it does offer compliance matrices and annotated outlines. However, its outputs are not grounded in a firm-specific Data Library the way GovDash drafts are, and GovEagle's scope stops at proposal-stage tasks without extending into capture, pricing, or contract data. For teams that want a single system to carry a pursuit from solicitation analysis through compliant draft submission, GovEagle requires pairing with a separate proposal tool. GovDash covers that entire range without a handoff. Lifecycle Scope: Capture, Pricing, and Contract Management GovDash covers the full arc of the contract lifecycle, from early opportunity pursuit through final contract management. GovEagle focuses on proposal generation and opportunity intelligence but does not extend into pricing, contract management, or post-award tracking. Within GovDash, capture management software lets capture teams track pursuits, build out competitive analysis, and develop win strategies before a solicitation even drops. Once an RFP is released, the same data flows directly into proposal development without re-entry. GovDash Pricer handles cost volume construction, and the contract management module takes over post-award, tracking deliverables, modifications, and compliance obligations. Here is how the two products compare across lifecycle stages: For contractors who need a single system that carries work from pipeline through post-award, GovEagle requires supplemental tools to cover the gaps. GovDash users avoid that context-switching because BD, capture, proposal, and contract data all live in one place. Security and Data Infrastructure Both GovDash and GovEagle operate in a space where data handling and security posture genuinely matter. Federal agencies increasingly review how vendor tools interact with sensitive procurement data, and contractors working on classified or sensitive programs need to know where their information lives. GovDash is built around NIST SP 800-171 alignment and has earned FedRAMP Ready designation . Full FedRAMP Authorization has not yet been achieved, so teams with active ATO-dependent requirements should verify current status before use. The system is audited by a C3PAO and stores all customer data in a dedicated, isolated environment. Proposal content, past performance records, and pricing data in your Data Library never train shared models or bleed into other customer workflows. GovEagle references NIST 800-53 alignment and zero data retention in its public materials, and is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate Equivalency, but has not completed a C3PAO audit or earned formal FedRAMP authorization. Teams with active ATO requirements should verify current status directly with GovEagle before committing to either system. Contractors who operate under DOD contracts, CUI handling requirements, or agency-specific data protection mandates should treat this table as a starting checklist, not a final compliance determination. GovDash vs. GovEagle: Feature Comparison at a Glance Here is a side-by-side breakdown of where each product stands across the capabilities that matter most to government contractors comparing AI tools for capture and proposal work. Proposal Development GovDash reads the solicitation, extracts Section L and M requirements, and maps them to a compliance matrix before generating a first draft. Drafts pull directly from the contractor's Data Library, so outputs are grounded in past performance, resumes, and prior technical volumes instead of generic web content. Teams working on large full-and-open competitions regularly cut first-draft generation from three to five days down to four to eight hours. GovEagle focuses on proposal generation as well, but its outputs are less tightly integrated with a firm's existing content assets. Capture and Pipeline Management GovDash monitors SAM.gov and other federal sources continuously, surfaces relevant opportunities, and logs them against your pursuit tracker automatically. That replaces roughly six to ten hours per week of manual pipeline research per BD FTE. Teams researching dedicated federal pipeline management tools can compare the leading options in that category. GovEagle does not include opportunity tracking or capture workflow capabilities; its focus is on proposal-stage tasks only. Feature Comparison Table Why GovDash is the Better Choice GovDash was built exclusively for government contractors, and that focus shows across every part of the product. title: From Input to Impact: Secure AI Where It Runs
summary: Defend the entire AI agentic stack across endpoints, identities, cloud, and apps with SentinelOne's unified platform.
body_text: AI agents have made their way into virtually every layer of your environment. They run in the apps your employees adopt, on the endpoints where agents execute code, as users with access privileges those agents borrow, and in the cloud workloads that scale them. The platform that you trust to secure your endpoints is already already covering where AI operates today. Here is the through-line that makes this one problem instead of four. Every AI attack starts as an interaction and ends as an action. A prompt gets manipulated, an agent gets tricked, and the damage lands on a host, reaches into an identity, or moves through the cloud. The tools that treat each surface as a separate product hand you fragments. SentinelOne treats them as one chain. How SentinelOne Defends the Agentic Stack Today Employee AI use is where the risk quietly enters. Your people are already using AI tools you never sanctioned, through browser, IDE, and API-connected apps and agentic AI tools. SentinelOne discovers that shadow AI use across browsers, IDEs, and copilots, highlights which tools and models are in play and governs it with policy. It keeps confidential data, PII, and secrets from reaching untrusted models, and it stops prompt injection and jailbreaks aimed at the tools you build. Legacy DLP reads patterns; this reads context, which is the only way to catch an attack aimed at AI systems that behave in a non-deterministic way. The agent layer is where AI stops advising and starts acting. An employee’s prompt sends text. An agent sends commands, holds credentials, calls APIs, and chain actions without a human approving each step. That makes them non-human identities with standing access. SentinelOne governs that access. It inventories the agents and MCP servers already operating and scores what each one can reach and holds every agent to the privileges its task requires. Then it inspects the tool calls themselves, so an injected instruction gets blocked at the moment it would execute. What gets executed lands in a searchable record, and the same enforcement doubles as a kill switch. Inventory the agents already running in your environment, the connectors they reach, and every tool call they make. While governance decides what an agent is allowed to do, the endpoint is where you find out what it actually did. The endpoint is where agents execute. This is the frontier, and where SentinelOne has protected customers for over a decade. Our behavioral engine judges what a process does, not what it claims to be. That is how we caught QUIETVAULT – malware that spins up AI agents in “yolo” mode to exfiltrate secrets to GitHub. It is how we autonomously stopped the LiteLLM supply chain attack, where adversaries weaponized the Claude CLI to install a malicious payload. It is how we surfaced a DLL side-loading attack hidden inside an AI tool installer. Real detections, on the endpoint, today. Agents run on the host, and so do we. The identity is where a hijacked agent runs next. Picture an employee’s AI coding agent that gets hijacked mid-task. It spawns a shell and reaches for cached credentials and cloud session tokens, trying to stop being a process and start being the user. That pivot to identity is what unlocks lateral movement, and it is where most AI attacks are headed. SentinelOne meets the move . It secures human and non-human identities alike, and seeds the environment with decoy credentials and honeytokens no legitimate user ever touches. The instant the hijacked agent grabs one, the trap trips, and Identity responds by forcing an MFA re-challenge, disabling the account, or isolating the host. Authorization at login is not enough. Access gets validated against behavior and pulled at runtime. The cloud is where AI workloads scale. Consider an internal AI agent running in a Kubernetes cluster with standing access to a customer database. Security teams keep asking the same question about deployments like this. Where is the model connecting, and who is it talking to? SentinelOne answers with eBPF-native runtime protection that judges how the workload actually behaves, and flags the moment that inference service reaches an endpoint it has never touched before. It covers the control plane the deployment depends on, the secrets it reads, the pipelines it runs through, and the data it can access. Defending the AI you build takes more than watching it, it takes action on the workload in real time. SentinelOne’s Singularity Platform Advantage Each of these surfaces matters on its own. What closes the kill chain is following an attack across them without losing it at the handoff. This is where a single platform earns its keep. AI telemetry already streams into the Singularity™ Data Lake , alongside the endpoint data the platform has correlated for years. As identity and cloud signals join that same view, an analyst follows one attack from first prompt to final action, without stitching logs across six tools at two in the morning. A manipulated prompt, the process it spawns, the credential it reaches for, and the cloud resource it targets read as one story rather than six disconnected alerts. Detection that only watches is observation. Runtime action is protection. When the Singularity Platform acts, autonomous response blocks the execution, rolls back the change, and revokes the access at the point of impact, without a human relaying orders between consoles. This is the difference between whether an attack is stopped or just gets logged. That is the case for securing AI inside a platform built for autonomous runtime response. We are not adding a console to chase AI, we are extending the one already deployed where your agents run. Does the solution protect the endpoint where agents actually execute, or is it a roadmap item? When a hijacked agent pivots to credentials and the cloud, does that telemetry land in the same platform, or are you manually connecting dots across three dashboards? Can the solution act at the moment of execution, or only tell me what already happened? SentinelOne protects the surfaces where AI runs today. This includes the apps your employees use, the agents they deploy, the endpoints where agents execute, the identities they borrow, and the cloud where they scale. One platform, built for autonomous response. While AI has changed the attack, it does not have to change your architecture. See it for yourself. title: Are Humans Naturally Monogamous? What Science Reveals About Love, Commitment and Pair Bonding

body_text: The truth about human relationships is more complicated than “made for one person forever” For generations, monogamy has been presented as the natural foundation of human relationships. Many societies view lifelong sexual and emotional exclusivity as the ideal model for love, marriage and family life. Yet human behaviour tells a more complicated story. Across history and cultures, people have formed relationships in many different ways, including lifelong partnerships, serial monogamy, open relationships, polygamous arrangements and periods of casual dating. This raises an important scientific question: are humans biologically designed for strict monogamy, or is monogamy a social system that humans choose to maintain? Research suggests the answer is somewhere in the middle. Humans appear to have a powerful ability to form deep pair bonds, but our biology and behaviour also show flexibility. Monogamy is uncommon in the animal world Compared with many mammals, humans are unusual. Long-term pair bonding is relatively rare across the animal kingdom. Scientists estimate that only a small percentage of mammal species form lasting partnerships. Among primates, long-term bonds are more common, but our closest relatives provide an interesting comparison. Chimpanzees and bonobos generally do not form sexually exclusive lifelong partnerships. Instead, they often have multiple sexual relationships within their social groups. Bonobos, in particular, use sexual behaviour as part of social bonding, conflict reduction and group cooperation. Their relationships demonstrate that sexuality in primates can serve many social purposes beyond reproduction. So why did humans develop such a strong tendency toward pair bonding? Why might monogamy have evolved? Scientists have proposed several explanations for the development of human monogamy. One major theory suggests that pair bonding evolved because it benefited children. Human infants require an unusually long period of care and development compared with many other animals. A committed partner who provides protection, food and support can increase the chances of offspring survival. Another evolutionary explanation focuses on protection. Research examining primate behaviour has suggested that in some species, males remain close to females and offspring because this reduces threats from competing males. There is also the possibility that monogamy developed because cooperation between partners improved access to resources. Sharing childcare, food gathering and protection may have created advantages for early human communities. However, evolution does not mean humans are programmed to behave in only one way. Instead, it means certain behaviours became useful under particular conditions. Pair bonding does not always mean strict monogamy A common misunderstanding is that forming a strong romantic bond automatically equals complete sexual exclusivity. Biologists often separate monogamy into different categories: Social monogamy: two individuals live together, cooperate and raise children as a pair. Sexual monogamy: two individuals have sexual relationships only with each other. Reproductive monogamy: two individuals reproduce exclusively together. In humans, these categories do not always overlap perfectly. A couple may build a strong emotional partnership while facing challenges around sexual exclusivity. Others may maintain sexual exclusivity but have different forms of emotional connection outside the relationship. According to bioanthropologist Agustín Fuentes, humans have a remarkable capacity for strong social and romantic bonds, but those bonds do not always follow one universal pattern. The science of love and attachment Human attachment is strongly influenced by brain chemistry. Studies of prairie voles, small mammals known for forming lasting partnerships, have shown the importance of chemicals such as oxytocin and vasopressin in creating social bonds. These chemicals influence feelings of trust, attachment and reward. Humans also experience powerful biological responses during romantic bonding. Brain imaging studies have shown that romantic love activates areas linked with motivation, pleasure and reward. This helps explain why people can experience intense attachment and commitment. However, the existence of these bonding systems does not automatically guarantee lifelong exclusivity. Human brains appear designed for connection, cooperation and attachment, but culture and personal choices influence how those instincts are expressed. What do human relationships look like in reality? Measuring human monogamy is difficult. Researchers face challenges because people do not always accurately report their romantic or sexual histories. Social expectations can influence what individuals are willing to disclose. Instead of only studying reported behaviour, some scientists have examined family patterns through genetics and anthropology. Research led by evolutionary anthropologist Mark Dyble analysed sibling relationships across human societies and compared them with other mammals. The findings suggested that humans show a strong tendency toward monogamous family structures, but not complete exclusivity. The study found that humans fit within the group of socially monogamous mammals. However, the results also showed that humans are more flexible than species that maintain almost complete reproductive exclusivity. This supports the idea that humans are neither completely monogamous nor naturally designed for constant multiple partnerships. Culture plays a major role in shaping relationships Human relationship patterns are influenced by much more than biology. Religion, laws, economic systems, inheritance traditions and social expectations have all shaped ideas about marriage and commitment. In many modern societies, monogamy is strongly connected to legal and cultural structures. At the same time, the meaning of monogamy has changed. For many people today, it no longer means one partner for an entire lifetime. Instead, it may mean one committed relationship at a time, with people experiencing several long-term relationships throughout their lives. This pattern is often described as serial monogamy. Different people also experience monogamy differently. For some, exclusive commitment feels natural and fulfilling. For others, it may require ongoing communication, effort and negotiation. Are humans really built for monogamy? The evidence suggests that humans are capable of monogamy, but strict lifelong sexual exclusivity is not a simple biological certainty. We have evolved strong abilities for attachment, love, cooperation and long-term partnership. These traits helped humans survive and raise children in complex social groups. At the same time, human behaviour shows flexibility. People create different relationship structures depending on their values, environments and cultural backgrounds. Rather than being naturally designed for either complete monogamy or complete non-monogamy, humans appear to be a species that can form deep bonds while adapting those bonds to different circumstances. The most accurate description may be that humans are naturally capable of monogamy, but not automatically limited to it. Love, commitment and partnership are not controlled by biology alone. They are shaped by a combination of evolution, society, personal decisions and individual experiences. Sources and Further Reading Fuentes, A. Race, Monogamy, and Other Lies They Told You . Scientific research on human relationships, evolution and behaviour continues to develop, and individual experiences may differ significantly from population-level findings. The information presented here should not be considered relationship advice, psychological guidance or a substitute for professional support.

title: D&G Light Blue vs Dior Sauvage: Which Should You Wear?
summary: D&G Light Blue vs Dior Sauvage: two of the most recommended starter fragrances compared on notes, longevity, and projection, so you know which one actually suits you.
body_text: Dior Sauvage and D&G Light Blue show up in the same searches for one practical reason: both get handed to first-time fragrance shoppers as the “safe” pick, one steered toward men, one toward women, and plenty of people want proof that the advice actually holds up before they commit a full bottle to either name. D&G Light Blue, available to try on Scentbird. D&G Light Blue vs Dior Sauvage: the similarities Set the gender marketing aside and the overlap is real. Both are freshness-first fragrances designed to read as effortless rather than complicated, both were built to be worn from morning through evening without a second thought, and both became so widely recommended that they turned into shorthand for “safe first bottle.” Neither one asks the wearer to think hard about the occasion, which is exactly why both keep showing up on best-seller lists years after launch. D&G Light Blue D&G Light Blue opens like a crate of citrus set down on warm stone: sharp Sicilian lemon and a bite of tart green apple, the kind of brightness that smells more like fruit than perfume. Composed by Olivier Cresp for Dolce and Gabbana in 2001, it settles into a soft bellflower and jasmine heart with a whisper of bamboo, then rests on light cedar, musk, and a touch of amber that keeps the whole thing from turning sugary. It belongs to the woody fruity family, and the wood only ever plays a supporting role. Expect four to six hours of wear that stays close to the skin, so a midday reapplication is part of the deal rather than a flaw. Skip it if you want a scent that someone across the room can pick up on, because Light Blue was never built to travel that far. Dior Sauvage Sauvage, composed by François Demachy for Dior in 2015, opens with a peppery hit of Calabrian bergamot and Sichuan pepper, moves through a cool sweep of lavender, and lands on a smooth, almost mineral base built around ambroxan, the synthetic amber note responsible for its now-familiar skin-warm trail. It smells clean and radiant rather than gourmand or spicy, closer to salt air over cedar than to a traditional spice bottle. It isn’t part of the Scentbird lineup right now, though it’s worth knowing this comparison still holds if you’re deciding between the two characters before buying either one elsewhere. Expect 6 to 8 hours with projection that fills a room for the first few hours before settling in. The trade-off is how common that ambroxan trail has become, since it’s one of the most-worn scents of the past decade, so it can feel less like a personal signature than a familiar one. Skip it if you’re hoping for something a stranger won’t immediately recognize. D&G Light Blue vs Dior Sauvage: notes, longevity, and projection D&G Light Blue Dior Sauvage Feel Sunlit citrus, crisp and fruity Peppery, radiant, mineral-amber Main notes Sicilian lemon, apple, jasmine, cedar Bergamot, pepper, lavender, ambroxan Lasts About 4 to 6 hours, close to skin About 6 to 8 hours, fills a room Best for Warm-weather daytime, casual wear All-day wear, versatile day to night Which one is better, D&G Light Blue or Dior Sauvage? The real differentiator here is presence, not quality. Light Blue is a light citrus accessory that asks to be noticed only by the person wearing it, while Sauvage is built to hold a room and stay there for most of the day. Choosing between them comes down to whether you want a scent that disappears politely by afternoon or one that announces itself and keeps going. The short answer Reach for D&G Light Blue when you want a bright, low-key citrus that never overstays its welcome, and accept the midday touch-up as part of the trade. Reach for Sauvage when you want one application to carry you through a full day with noticeable projection, and accept that it will smell familiar to a lot of people. If you’re still torn on which mood belongs in your rotation, the cheapest way to settle it is to try the one you can actually sample first. Put a month between you and the decision before buying full size. Try D&G Light Blue with Scentbird New to Scentbird? Take the fragrance quiz . Frequently asked questions What does D&G Light Blue smell like? D&G Light Blue smells like fresh-cut Sicilian lemon and green apple laid over a soft bellflower and jasmine heart, finished with light cedar and musk. It reads bright, clean, and fruity rather than sweet, closer to a citrus orchard than a florist’s counter. The whole effect stays close to the skin instead of filling a room. What does Dior Sauvage smell like? Sauvage opens with a peppery bergamot snap, moves through lavender, and settles into a smooth, almost mineral woody-amber base built around ambroxan. It smells clean and radiant rather than sweet or spicy in the traditional sense. That ambroxan base is what gives it the long, skin-warm trail it is known for. Which lasts longer, D&G Light Blue or Dior Sauvage? Sauvage lasts noticeably longer, typically 6 to 8 hours with real projection that carries into a room. Light Blue tends to run 4 to 6 hours and stays close to the skin, often needing a reapplication by midafternoon. If all-day, no-touch-up wear matters most, Sauvage has the clear edge. Is D&G Light Blue too light to wear next to something as strong as Sauvage? Not at all, they simply serve different moments. Light Blue is built for warm-weather, low-key daytime wear where a loud trail would feel like too much. Sauvage is the one to reach for when you want a scent that holds its ground for a full day. Can I try Dior Sauvage through Scentbird? Sauvage isn’t part of the Scentbird lineup right now, so this comparison is meant to help you decide on character and performance before buying it elsewhere. D&G Light Blue is available to try on Scentbird, which makes it the easier of the two to sample in a low-commitment vial first. Which one is the better everyday, office-friendly scent? Light Blue tends to work better in small, shared spaces since it sits close to the skin and never overwhelms a room. Sauvage is easy to wear too, but its stronger projection means a lighter hand is worth using around a desk or an elevator. title: HR Burnout Is Higher Than Ever. Is AI the Cause?
summary: Google search interest in HR burnout is up 3,500%, right as AI adoption spiked. Data from BCG and Deloitte reveals what's actually driving it.
body_text: Searches for “HR burnout” have jumped about 3,500% over the past year, according to Google Trends. That climb lines up almost exactly with AI’s rapid arrival inside HR’s job description, both as a tool HR is expected to use and as a rollout HR is expected to lead for everyone else. When you see these trends together, the question asks itself: Is AI the reason? HR professionals are experiencing burnout at higher rates than the employees they support Mind Share Partners’ 2025 Mental Health at Work Report , run with Qualtrics, found that 54% of HR professionals report moderate to severe burnout, compared to 48% of non-HR employees. Lattice’s 2026 State of People Strategy Report found that 48% of U.S. HR practitioners are considering leaving the field entirely, citing the emotional toll of managing employee issues, feeling undervalued, and the collapse of work-life balance. So what’s driving this? Examining AI’s Role in HR Burnout On paper, AI looks like exactly what tipped this over. OpenAI’s research on how AI is expanding what people do at work analyzed over 800,000 ChatGPT conversations from U.S. workers and found that HR has one of the highest rates of “task crossover” of any function measured, with 69% of its AI use going toward work outside HR’s traditional scope. HR is already the department stretching furthest, covering ground a helpful tool was supposed to close. And what AI actually handed HR was not small. The Coders Guild found that 95% of HR leaders report rising workloads, and 91% say their responsibilities grew over the past year specifically because of AI-related work: workforce planning, employee training, governance, recruitment redesign, and organizational change. Rather than simply adopting a new tool, HR professionals have effectively taken on a second job. Blame the tool, and you’ll fix the wrong thing Here is where the easy answer of “blaming AI” falls apart. Deloitte’s 2026 Human Capital Trends found that companies taking a technology-first approach to AI are 1.6 times more likely to miss the returns they expected than companies that lead with a human-centric approach. Prosci’s research on AI change management backs this up from the failure side: 43% of organizations point to insufficient executive sponsorship as the reason their AI rollout stalled, 38% point to inadequate training, and 63% cite human factors, not technical ones, as the primary obstacle. Taken together, these findings shift the focus. The issue is not AI itself, but insufficient leadership during implementation. Companies have overlooked the human aspects of the rollout, leaving HR to manage both the resulting gaps and consequences. HR is leaning in anyway Despite these challenges, HR professionals remain optimistic about AI. Lattice found that 83% of HR professionals feel excitement, hope, or optimism about delegating tasks to AI, and 42% use it regularly. Even still, The Coders Guild reports that only 23% of HR departments have received AI-specific training. HR continues to lead in adoption, yet receives very little support. HR should keep leading AI adoption ; what needs to change is taking away some legacy work, like compliance paperwork , so new responsibilities don’t compete with old ones. So, is AI the cause? Not quite. The data points to something more specific: when AI is added without executive support, training, or reducing old workloads, it’s not a productivity tool. It’s just another job. Giving this extra work to a group already facing 54% burnout, without easing their original duties, makes the huge jump in “HR burnout” searches less of a mystery and starts looking like the most predictable workplace outcome.

title: $2.1 Million Gets You a Museum-Quality 2006 Ford GT Heritage
summary: When an online auction generates over 1000 comments, it’s probably one worth paying attention to. This past week, one comment section swelled to a mind-numbing 1780 chime-ins. The commenters had time to chat, too, since the auction extended roughly two hours after its scheduled end time. Two bidders kept upping the ante in thousand-dollar increments, […]
body_text: When an online auction generates over 1000 comments, it’s probably one worth paying attention to. This past week, one comment section swelled to a mind-numbing 1780 chime-ins. The commenters had time to chat, too, since the auction extended roughly two hours after its scheduled end time. Two bidders kept upping the ante in thousand-dollar increments, each time resetting the sale’s two-minute timer. The impact to all 2005–06 Ford GTs out there is being felt—two Ford GT owners in the comments committed to hugging their cars after this auction ended. These are likely normal, downright rational actions when history is made in such a radical fashion. The auction in question resulted in a $2,108,500 final price, including fees, for a 2006 Ford GT Heritage Edition. But just because one example skyrockets to the moon doesn’t mean they all do. And time has proven that prices for Ford GTs with the Gulf livery theme are the ones to get, especially when they have fewer than 10 miles on the odometer. This could be an expensive outlier, but it’s still part of a larger trend in appreciation of Ford’s two-year Supercar tribute in celebration of its 100th Anniversary. We previously noted a 35% increase in 2005–06 Ford GT values over the last quarter, but we never expected a Heritage Edition with delivery miles would exceed our $1.3M median valuation (in #1, or concours condition) by nearly a million bucks. hymanltd | Bring A Trailer hymanltd | Bring A Trailer hymanltd | Bring A Trailer The Gulf racing livery on the Heritage Edition package is universally admired, and it was a one-year-only option valued at $13,000. That was nearly 10% of the GT’s base price ($139,995) at the time, but it was a popular add-on, and a large portion of production (343 units) was dedicated to the Heritage. Considering 2011 units were sold in 2006, the Heritage is almost a high-volume configuration. There were more acute rarities made, including a one-off with silver racing stripes. Production was also minuscule for examples with conventional paint jobs but without the central racing stripe or the side stripes. So it’s fair to chalk up this valuation high-water mark to the long shadow cast by Gulf Oil. And the fact that almost nobody drove this Ford GT for distances measured in units larger than yards, as this example retains all its assembly line markings and was never “dealer prepped” for a retail sale. A “wrapper car,” indeed. hymanltd | Bring A Trailer hymanltd | Bring A Trailer hymanltd | Bring A Trailer While the plastic square over the airbag’s emblem could be original, this unit also has no outstanding recalls according to NHTSA. That suggests the previous owner ensured Ford went out of their way to install a replacement airbag without putting any mileage on the odometer. (There are reports of Ford towing affected vehicles to dealerships, and hiring third-party contractors to perform airbag swaps at the owner’s residence.) The Ford GT Community is tight, and low-mile Heritage GTs are well known. I personally saw a 2006 Ford GT Heritage owned by a local dealer magnate and car collector , who stored his in museum condition and claimed it only had 2 miles on it. There was also a 2.4-mile Heritage GT that sold for $533,000 for everyone to see back in 2020, suggesting these modest odometer figures are far from a one-off occurrence. hymanltd | Bring A Trailer hymanltd | Bring A Trailer hymanltd | Bring A Trailer The 2005–06 Ford GT, famously dubbed the “Pace Car for an Entire Company,” came from a unique moment in time, when a bespoke platform could be made in a low-volume Ford factory dedicated to other prestigious automobiles. It had an engine with the best traits of the SVT Cobra and the Lincoln Navigator, and the parts-swapping inside and out was downright challenging to spot. Its styling and layout were a clear nod to the GT40 of the ’60s, but it was also a legit supercar in its own right and not just an empty retro tribute. It was also delightfully analog, something increasingly rare just a generation later. A car with the Ford GT’s blue-ovaled pedigree can never exist again, because the company that made it looks completely different today. This sale further shows just how kindly history is looking upon this unique creation. The two Heritage GT owners mentioned above, and possibly every Ford GT owner out there, surely have what transpired this past week on the brain. But one $2.1M sale does not necessarily make the market. Other low-mile GTs will come up for sale in the coming months, which is when we’ll really see how high these cars can go. title: Automating Campaign Operations: Triggering Payouts via API Webhooks
summary: Struggling to pay hundreds of creators or canvassers on time? See how payout API webhooks trigger instant payments the moment a milestone is verified.
body_text: Scaling a campaign to thousands of micro-creators or field canvassers shouldn't mean drowning in manual payment approvals. This piece looks at how connecting event webhooks directly to a payouts API lets marketing platforms and civic tech teams trigger payments the moment a milestone is verified, cutting out the operational drag that manual dashboard uploads create. Every campaign manager who has tried to pay a few thousand micro-influencers or door-to-door canvassers by hand knows the drill. Someone exports a spreadsheet of verified actions, cross-checks it against a folder of screenshots or a CRM report, then keys in payout amounts one by one. It works when a campaign is paying twenty people. It falls apart at two thousand. This isn't just an inconvenience, it's a measurable drag on how fast a campaign can move. The workforce behind these campaigns is also growing quickly. In its 2024 Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking, the Federal Reserve found that roughly one in five U.S. adults had done some form of gig or task-based work in the prior month, a pool that increasingly overlaps with the micro-creators and part-time canvassers that civic campaigns and marketing platforms rely on. That's a lot of people expecting to be paid promptly, and manual payout processes were never built to keep pace with that kind of scale. What are Payout API Webhooks and How Do They Work? A payout API webhook is a notification that fires the instant something happens in an existing system, then triggers an action in a payments platform without anyone touching a dashboard. If a canvasser submits a validated voter registration form, or a creator's post crosses a verified engagement threshold, that event can call a webhook that instructs a payouts API to send funds automatically. This is a different way of thinking about disbursements. Instead of collecting a week's worth of activity and uploading it as one file, each qualifying action becomes its own trigger. The payout logic lives in code, tied to the same conditions a team already uses to measure success, whether that's a form submission, a milestone in a CRM, or an engagement count pulled from a social platform. How Do Payout API Webhooks Cut Operational Costs? Event-driven systems like this aren't just faster, they're also cheaper to run than manual workflows. Gartner's research into event-driven architecture found that a majority of IT leaders, 68% according to a recent poll, are planning to increase their use of this model, largely because it removes the need for teams to manually reconcile and re-key data between systems. For a campaign paying out thousands of small, frequent amounts, that translates into fewer hours spent on spreadsheet cleanup and fewer errors that require follow-up corrections. Speed matters just as much as cost here. Freelance and gig income is already irregular, and research summarized by research found that 84% of freelancers would choose an instant payment option if one were available. When a campaign's payout process can't keep up with its own growth, the result is often disengaged talent, missed compliance windows, and finance teams stuck reconciling spreadsheets instead of running the program. Is it Safe to Automate Contractor Payments with Webhooks? Automation only helps if it's paired with the right guardrails. A well-built payouts API doesn't just move money faster, it also handles the identity verification, tax form collection, and risk checks that keep a payout compliant before it ever leaves the account. That matters more, not less, once payments are triggered automatically, since there's no manual reviewer catching a mismatched name or an incomplete W-9 before funds go out. The practical answer is that automated payouts can be safer than manual ones, provided the underlying platform builds compliance into the trigger itself rather than treating it as a separate step. A payout that only fires once identity and tax requirements are satisfied removes the temptation to skip verification when a campaign is under deadline pressure. Choosing a Payments Partner Built for Campaign Speed This is where Dots fits into the picture. Instead of forcing teams to choose between speed and compliance, Dots' event-driven architecture ties payouts directly to internal software logic or third-party webhooks, so a verified post, a completed canvassing form, or a milestone in an existing system can release payment automatically, while identity verification, 1099 collection, and risk checks run in the background. That's a meaningful shift from legacy payout APIs and traditional wire transfers, which typically require a person to initiate every transaction and offer little room to route payments intelligently across 190-plus countries and 135-plus currencies . Getting started also doesn't require an enterprise-sized commitment. Dots' Core plan starts at $19 a month and already includes API access, domestic and international payouts, ID verification, and 1099 tax compliance, which covers most of what a growing campaign or platform needs to automate its first webhook-triggered payout flow. Teams that outgrow that setup can move into higher tiers with white-labeled experiences and dedicated support, but there's no need to overspend just to get the automation benefits working from day one. If manual dashboard uploads are holding back how fast a campaign can scale, it may be worth looking at what a webhook-triggered payout flow could do instead.
